plan.summary: Add `</th` and `</tr` to the sentence-boundary tag set in negationSentenceSpans, so a table header row does not scan as one sentence containing raw markup. Two tests, one mutation-proven.

edits.rationale: `</th` is not reachable via the `</h` arm (third character differs) and its sibling `</td` was already present, so header cells were the only cell type that did not close a span. `</tr` added as insurance for rows with unclosed cells. Comment records why `</h` does not cover it, because that is the exact reasoning error that would remove it again.

plan.risks:
NARROWING A SENTENCE IS THE SAFE DIRECTION, but it is not free: a span that previously ran across a header boundary now ends earlier, so a construction that genuinely spanned two header cells would no longer be detected. That is correct - a define-by-negation construction split across two table cells is not one sentence, and repairing it as though it were is what produces the markup-eating splice.

NO EFFECT ON EXISTING CONTENT until something re-renders: this changes detection at write time, so already-stored copy is untouched. The gate's exemption and budget behaviour are unchanged.

NOT A COMPLETE HTML PARSER, stated plainly: the boundary set is a prefix list, not a grammar. Other block-level closers (</blockquote, </dd, </dt, </caption, </section) are still absent. They are not added here because none of them is currently produced into these slots by RULE 10, and adding untested prefixes on speculation is how the `</th`/`</td` asymmetry arose in the first place. If RULE 10 later gains one, it needs the same probe and the same fixture.

UNCHANGED BY THIS: the scanner still splits on punctuation as well as tags, which is what makes the peer's list-without-terminators case work correctly today.
